metadata.title: Does a Clean NDA Review Mean It's Safe to Sign?
metadata.purpose: Answer whether an NDA review that comes back with nothing flagged means the NDA is safe to sign, or only once every flagged clause is checked against the law that applies. Lands the carry-out that a clean review is not a green light, and a heavily flagged one is not a red one, until someone checks the flagged clauses.

beats.narration_text: The obvious guess: Claude CLEARS the NDA — a final legal sign-off. Wrong word. Claude REVIEWS it, checking every clause against a baseline of standard terms and flagging what's off. Take it apart.

beats.narration_text: Here's what's tempting: an NDA review flags nothing, therefore the NDA is fine. Follow the logic through, though. Say the confidentiality clause never carves out information that later becomes public through no fault of anyone — a competitor publishes it first. On the page, that clause reads like a complete, ordinary definitions section, sitting right next to other clauses that do include the standard carve-outs. Nothing gets flagged because nothing on the page is unusual. A review optimized to catch what's off in the text can't catch what's simply absent from it.

shot.new_visual_element: An NDA page dense with clauses; one clause gets circled in accent, then struck, with a caption revealing what's missing

production_viz.label: A complete-looking clause, quietly missing one thing
production_viz.mechanic: An NDA page densely filled with clause lines. One line reading a confidentiality definition gets circled in accent color, then struck through as a caption fades in below: 'no carve-out for public info.' The page's border flashes accent, not from an error in the drafting, but from what almost got waved through as complete.

beats.narration_text: A working NDA review has three moving parts. Clauses go in. A baseline of standard terms — definitions, carve-outs, duration, mutuality — sits in the middle. What's unusual against that baseline comes out as a flag list. That's the machine. Watch the anchor: that same confidentiality clause comes back stamped in the margin. Not a verdict. Not confirmed a problem. Flagged: no carve-out for public information. The word 'flagged' is doing precise work here — it means look at this, not reject this.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR -- three labeled parts lighting in turn (clauses / baseline / flag list), then an NDA clause stamped FLAGGED -- NO CARVE-OUT

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR -- three parts, then the clause
production_viz.mechanic: Three chips fade in one at a time across the top, each labelled with a part of a working NDA review (clauses / baseline / flag list), then fade out together. THE ANCHOR. A clean, short NDA clause appears -- a confidentiality definition, one line visible -- with a stamp across the margin reading 'FLAGGED -- NO CARVE-OUT' in bold. THIS EXACT CLAUSE RETURNS, CHECKED, AT B03.

beats.narration_text: The flagged clause goes to someone who knows the law that actually applies — reasonable carve-out, reasonable duration, mutuality: those aren't properties of the clause alone, they're properties of the clause plus the jurisdiction plus the deal. Only after that check does flagged move to fine after all, or to something that has to change. Now the trade-off cuts both ways. Nothing flagged doesn't mean nothing's wrong — the review only catches gaps against its baseline, and a clause sitting outside that baseline slips through clean. And a heavily flagged NDA isn't automatically a bad deal — 'flagged' means check this, not reject this. The whole thing is optimized to surface what deserves a lawyer's eye, at the expense of ever handing you a straight yes.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR RETURNS -- the flagged clause gets checked and the page is stamped CHECKED -- OK TO SIGN; then splits into 'no flag is not nothing wrong' and 'flagged is not reject it'

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR RETURNS -- flagged, then checked
production_viz.mechanic: THE B02 CLAUSE RETURNS, identical placement, its 'FLAGGED -- NO CARVE-OUT' stamp crossed out and replaced with a checkmark and a new stamp reading 'CHECKED -- OK TO SIGN'. It splits into two cards: left reads 'no flag shown' with a struck-through 'NOTHING WRONG' beneath it labelled 'no flag is not nothing wrong'; right reads 'heavily flagged' with a checkmark beneath it labelled 'flagged is not reject it'.

beats.narration_text: A clean NDA review is a first pass, not a verdict. The check is only real once someone reads the flagged clauses against the law that actually applies.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini: I want to understand what actually happens when an AI reviews the NDA I'm considering signing. Here's the NDA — paste it in. Walk me through your review as three separate outputs. First, the list of standard confidentiality carve-outs — public information, independent development, prior knowledge, legally required disclosure — and whether each one is present, missing, or ambiguous in this NDA. Second, anything you'd flag as unusual against a baseline of standard mutual NDAs, and why. Third, the specific questions I should ask a lawyer who knows the law that applies in my state and industry — because 'reasonable' isn't a property of the clause alone. Don't tell me whether to sign. Go deeper: paste the same NDA back in and ask the model to draft the exact edits — in track-changes form — that would close every gap it flagged. Now you have a redline you can hand to the other side, and something a lawyer can react to instead of build from scratch.

llm_exercise.prompt: I want to understand what actually happens when an AI reviews an NDA I'm considering signing. Here's the NDA: [paste the full text or the clauses you're worried about]. Walk me through your review as three separate outputs: (1) the list of standard confidentiality carve-outs — public information, independent development, prior knowledge, legally required disclosure — and whether each is present, missing, or ambiguous in this NDA; (2) any clause you'd flag as unusual against a baseline of standard mutual NDAs, and why; (3) the specific questions I should ask a lawyer who knows the law that applies in my state and industry — because 'reasonable' carve-out or duration depends on jurisdiction and deal type, not on the clause alone. Do not tell me whether to sign.
